title: Common Data Service API contract
description: Platform-independent structured Data Service API semantics for r2db-api and MitateDB-api. This is intentionally NOT an OpenAPI document: it is the source-of-truth semantic contract for both implementations. An OpenAPI surface may be derived from it, but this file remains authoritative; do not report the absence of OpenAPI structure as a defect.

application_credential.description: Opaque credential presented over TLS. The service stores only a verifier/digest and never returns the secret. CredentialIssued.secret -- and the secret a rotate response returns, wherever this contract defines one -- is the complete bearer token for the surface that credential is for: a client presents that exact string, verbatim, as Authorization: Bearer <secret>; an application credential on the application surface, a control or audit credential on the control surface (security.schemes.control_credential continues to state that application credentials are not accepted there). A client MUST NOT compose it from, split it into, or derive it from any other field of the response -- credential_id is returned as its own field, for naming the credential in later control operations, and is never something a client extracts from the secret. Its internal structure is opaque; an implementation may change that structure without a contract change, and no client may depend on it. The service still stores only a verifier/digest and never returns the secret again.

control_credential.description: A separately authenticated Control/Audit authority; application credentials are not accepted. The service stores only a verifier/digest; the secret is returned exactly once, at issue or rotate time. An authentication secret is never reused as signing-key or other cryptographic material. CredentialIssued.secret -- and the secret a rotate response returns, wherever this contract defines one -- is the complete bearer token for the surface that credential is for: a client presents that exact string, verbatim, as Authorization: Bearer <secret>; an application credential on the application surface, a control or audit credential on the control surface (security.schemes.control_credential continues to state that application credentials are not accepted there). A client MUST NOT compose it from, split it into, or derive it from any other field of the response -- credential_id is returned as its own field, for naming the credential in later control operations, and is never something a client extracts from the secret. Its internal structure is opaque; an implementation may change that structure without a contract change, and no client may depend on it. The service still stores only a verifier/digest and never returns the secret again.

security.scope: Application and role are derived from authoritative credential state; request fields cannot select either.
security.failure: Unknown, expired, revoked, disabled, or unavailable authorization state fails closed.

versioning.compatibility: Additive fields and capabilities are allowed; removal or semantic change requires a new major version. The control surface follows the same compatibility rules. A response or request schema closure (additionalProperties: false) that narrows what the schema accepts, applied only to stop a schema from implying the existence of a field an implementation does not actually return or accept, is compatible as a minor-version change under version_binding's version-declaration discipline below -- it is not the kind of removal or semantic change that would otherwise require a new major version, because it constrains the documentation of shape rather than removing a previously-required capability or altering accepted semantics.
versioning.discovery: GET /v1/capabilities returns the negotiated contract version, capabilities, roles, and finite limits.
versioning.control_discovery: Where the control plane is provided, GET /control/v1/capabilities returns the control surface's own capability document; a separately deployed control surface must not be assumed to share a host with /v1/capabilities, and /v1/capabilities accepting control authority is a co-hosting convenience, not a requirement.
versioning.unknown_capability: The service returns CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED without executing a fallback.
versioning.version_binding: An implementation's own declared contract_version is the general rule for which version's definitions it is claiming conformance to: only an implementation declaring 1.2.0 or higher claims conformance to the obligations 1.2.0 introduced -- exhaustively: (1) the destructive_confirmation section in full, (2) errors.details_vocabulary's LIMIT_EXCEEDED.limit_class requirement, (3) subordinate ruling 7(A)'s response/request schema closures (additionalProperties: false on every schema and definition this version lists as closed), and (4) capability_status.rules' limits/limit_enforcement vocabulary-restriction rule. Only an implementation declaring 1.3.0 or higher additionally claims conformance to the obligations 1.3.0 introduced (subordinate ruling 8): audit-role acceptance on the three read-only control endpoints (control_capabilities, list_applications, list_credentials) with FORBIDDEN fail-closed on every other control endpoint; the per-application issuance-freeze FORBIDDEN refusal; and the optional target_id audit field and optional must_rotate exposure -- both are optional fields, so declaring 1.3.0 does not require emitting either one, only that their documented semantics hold whenever they are emitted. Only an implementation declaring 1.4.0 or higher additionally claims conformance to the obligations 1.4.0 introduced (subordinate ruling 9). Three of those obligations are unconditional in the same sense as every obligation enumerated above -- they bind simply by declaring 1.4.0, independent of any capability's own status: (a) audit_events is a reserved entity/collection name an implementation may refuse a client schema/collection operation against (structured_operations.reserved_entity_names_note); (b) where a control surface is provided at all (control_plane other than unavailable, the same precondition subordinate ruling 8 already carries), an audit-role credential is additionally accepted on the audit_query control endpoint alongside the three read-only endpoints ruling 8 already named, with FORBIDDEN fail-closed on every other control endpoint unchanged -- this holds whether that implementation's own audit_query capability is itself enabled or unavailable, since route registration and role authorization there precede the capability-availability check (an unavailable audit_query still answers an authorized audit-role caller with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED, never FORBIDDEN or a bare 404). Added by a later revision of this document still under this same 1.4.0 label (subordinate ruling 10, item 2): this acceptance is scoped to the control surface's audit_query control endpoint (the canonical POST /control/v1/audit/query, and its alias as served on the control host -- the same host scoping endpoints.audit_query.deprecation_note already states, and this document's own 1.4.0 conditional obligation (5) below, which requires both paths to answer as the identical operation). A data-plane host is not thereby obliged to authenticate control or audit credentials merely because it declares control_plane as something other than unavailable; where such a host holds no control-credential store, it may refuse a control or audit credential presented on its own POST /v1/audit/query alias as an unknown credential (AUTH_INVALID); it is not thereby required to accept, verify, or forward it. Co-hosting both surfaces in one process remains permitted (versioning.control_discovery) and is not what this scoping addresses; and (c) audit_query's canonical classification in this document is control_endpoints (POST /control/v1/audit/query), with the pre-1.4.0 endpoints.audit_query path (POST /v1/audit/query) retained as an alias of the identical operation for one further minor version. The remaining 1.4.0 obligations are conditional, unlike every obligation enumerated above for earlier versions: they bind an implementation declaring 1.4.0 only insofar as that implementation's own capabilities() additionally declares audit_query as something other than unavailable, since whether audit_query is provided at all remains a capability-declared matter, not a version-mandated one (the same posture control_plane.provision already establishes for the control surface as a whole) -- an implementation may declare contract_version 1.4.0 while its own audit_query stays unavailable (for example, no audit datastore is configured for this deployment) and remains fully conformant to 1.4.0 throughout, without being held to, or claiming, any obligation in this conditional list while unavailable. Where an implementation does declare audit_query as enabled or partial, 1.4.0 additionally requires -- exhaustively: (1) AuditQueryRequest.after, when accepted, is treated as an opaque cursor encoding a position under the ordering in (2) rather than interpreted as an event_id or a numeric offset, and a value that fails to decode or no longer resolves under the request's own filters is answered with VALIDATION_FAILED; (2) AuditResult.events[] is returned in the total order (recorded_at, plane, event_id); (3) each returned event carries a plane field whose value is control or application; (4) event_class is a vocabulary the implementation itself declares (its own capabilities().audit_query.event_classes), not a fixed contract enum, and 1.4.0 requires no particular member of it; (5) both the canonical POST /control/v1/audit/query path and the POST /v1/audit/query alias actually answer requests as the identical operation, rather than one of the two being merely routed without a working handler behind it; and (6) where audit_requests_per_minute is published in limits/limit_enforcement, it governs the audit_query endpoint specifically, as its own declared and separately enforceable limit class, and is not satisfied by also enforcing control_requests_per_minute for audit_query requests. Only an implementation declaring 1.5.0 or higher additionally claims conformance to the obligation 1.5.0 introduces (subordinate ruling 10, item 1). Like 1.4.0's own conditional obligations, this one binds an implementation declaring 1.5.0 only insofar as that implementation's own capabilities() declares audit_query as something other than unavailable; an implementation may declare contract_version 1.5.0 while its own audit_query stays unavailable and remains fully conformant to 1.5.0 throughout, without being held to this obligation while unavailable. Since 1.5.0 (subordinate ruling 10, item 1, conditional): operations and target_kinds are vocabularies each implementation declares for itself at capabilities().audit_query.operations / .target_kinds -- the sets of values the operation and target_kind fields of events returned by audit_query can take. As with event_classes, this contract enumerates no fixed enum and requires no particular member (declare-the-hazard). An implementation declaring 1.5.0 or higher whose audit_query is other than unavailable MUST declare both, and every event it returns MUST carry values drawn from the declared sets; the same superset relation holds for event_classes, stated here explicitly. Only an implementation declaring 1.6.0 or higher additionally claims conformance to the obligations 1.6.0 introduces (subordinate ruling 11). Two of those obligations are unconditional in the same sense as every obligation enumerated above -- they bind simply by declaring 1.6.0, independent of any capability's own status: (a) its GET /v1/capabilities document carries surfaces.data.base_url, the absolute base URL of its own data surface, and -- where a control surface is provided at all (control_plane other than unavailable, the same precondition subordinate rulings 8 and 9 already carry) -- both surfaces' capability documents additionally carry surfaces.control.base_url, each document carrying the same surfaces; and (b) the secret returned by any issue or rotate path it offers, in band or out of band, is accepted verbatim as a bearer token on the surface that credential is for, with no composition, splitting, or derivation required of the client (security.schemes). The remaining 1.6.0 obligations are conditional, in the same sense 1.4.0's own conditional list is: they bind only insofar as the implementation's own capabilities() declares the named capability as something other than unavailable. Where it declares application_catalog as something other than unavailable: (1) every EntityDescriptor it returns carries field_types, total over that entity's own fields, reporting json for any field created without a declared type. Where it declares schema_operations as something other than unavailable: (2) a create_entity it executes accepts field_types and creates each field named there with the type declared there, and an add_field it executes accepts every member of the seven-member vocabulary, json included; a field_types naming a field outside the request's own fields, carrying a value outside that vocabulary, or sent without fields, is refused with VALIDATION_FAILED. 1.6.0 introduces no obligation on what a client must send: SchemaOperationRequest.field_types is optional wherever it appears, and a request valid under 1.5.0 stays valid. An implementation still declaring 1.5.0 is not held to any 1.6.0-only, 1.7.0-only, or 1.8.0-only obligation retroactively. Every obligation introduced under a given version label -- whether enumerated above or added by a later revision of this document still under that same label -- follows this same general rule. An implementation still declaring 1.1.0 remains conformant to 1.1.0 semantics and is not held to any 1.2.0-only, 1.3.0-only, 1.4.0-only, 1.5.0-only, 1.6.0-only, 1.7.0-only, or 1.8.0-only obligation retroactively, an implementation declaring 1.2.0 is not held to any 1.3.0-only, 1.4.0-only, 1.5.0-only, 1.6.0-only, 1.7.0-only, or 1.8.0-only obligation retroactively, an implementation declaring 1.3.0 is not held to any 1.4.0-only, 1.5.0-only, 1.6.0-only, 1.7.0-only, or 1.8.0-only obligation retroactively, and an implementation declaring 1.4.0 is not held to any 1.5.0-only, 1.6.0-only, 1.7.0-only, or 1.8.0-only obligation retroactively. Only an implementation declaring 1.7.0 or higher additionally claims conformance to the obligations 1.7.0 introduces (subordinate ruling 12). Two of those obligations are unconditional in the same sense as every obligation enumerated above -- they bind simply by declaring 1.7.0, independent of any capability's own status: (a) every denial it answers with VALIDATION_FAILED, IDENTIFIER_INVALID or CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED carries the details keys errors.details_vocabulary requires for that code, with violated_declaration drawn from the closed vocabulary named there, and carries no row value, no suggested value, no corrective action and no internal name; and (b) every successful QueryResult, MutationResult and SchemaOperationResult it returns carries request_id, the same identifier its own audit evidence for that request carries. The remaining 1.7.0 obligations are conditional, in the same sense 1.4.0's and 1.6.0's own conditional lists are: they bind only insofar as the implementation's own capabilities() declares the named capability -- or, where two are named, both of them -- as something other than unavailable. Where it declares constraint_declarations and schema_operations both as something other than unavailable: (1) a create_entity it executes accepts field_constraints, an add_field and an alter_field it executes accept enum and nullable, each field is created or altered with the constraints declared there, those constraints are enforced on every value written to that field, and an alter_field whose declared constraints existing rows would violate is refused in full with CONFLICT, changing nothing. Where it declares constraint_declarations and application_catalog both as something other than unavailable: (2) every EntityDescriptor it returns carries field_constraints, total over that entity's own fields, reporting nullable: true and no enum for a field that declares neither. Where it declares dry_run as something other than unavailable: (3) a request carrying dry_run receives the decision the identical request without it would receive -- the same code and the same details on a refusal, the same affected count on a success -- and leaves no externally visible state change, subject to the two consumptions structured_operations.dry_run.external_effects names; and a plan it returns is deterministic, and is verified by recomputation on the real request, refusing with PRECONDITION_FAILED where it no longer agrees. Where it declares idempotency as something other than unavailable: (4) an idempotency_key is recorded with a digest of the request it accompanied, in the same transaction as that request's own effects; the same key with the same digest, resent within idempotency_retention_ms, returns the original result without re-executing, including the original request_id; and the same key with a different digest is refused with CONFLICT. Where it declares request_budget as something other than unavailable: (5) a budget narrows a bound downward only, a budget above the deployed value or naming a class that does not apply to that endpoint is refused with VALIDATION_FAILED, and exceeding a narrowed bound is refused with LIMIT_EXCEEDED naming that limit class. 1.7.0 introduces no obligation on what a client must send: dry_run, plan, budget, field_constraints, enum, nullable, and SchemaOperationRequest.idempotency_key are optional wherever they appear, and a request valid under 1.6.0 stays valid. Only an implementation declaring 1.8.0 or higher additionally claims conformance to the obligations 1.8.0 introduces (subordinate ruling 13). One of those obligations is unconditional in the same sense as every obligation enumerated above -- it binds simply by declaring 1.8.0, independent of any capability's own status: every limit_enforcement value it publishes describes the whole deployment reachable at the declared surfaces base URL, never one server process, so it declares enforced for a limit class only when the bound holds across every process that may serve that base URL at the same time, and declares deployment_required when the bound is held per process and more than one process may serve that base URL. The remaining 1.8.0 obligation is conditional, in the same sense 1.4.0's, 1.6.0's and 1.7.0's own conditional lists are: it binds only insofar as the implementation's own capabilities() declares idempotency as something other than unavailable: (1) two requests carrying the same idempotency_key that arrive together are serialized so that at most one of them executes, the other being answered after the first commits as a resend -- from the record where the digests agree, with CONFLICT where they differ -- and the idempotency_entries bound is evaluated under that same serialization (structured_operations.idempotency.record). 1.8.0 introduces no obligation on what a client must send: a request valid under 1.7.0 stays valid. An implementation still declaring 1.6.0 is not held to any 1.7.0-only or 1.8.0-only obligation retroactively. An implementation still declaring 1.7.0 is not held to any 1.8.0-only obligation retroactively. Only an implementation declaring 1.9.0 or higher additionally claims conformance to the obligations 1.9.0 introduces (subordinate ruling 14). Those obligations are unconditional in the same sense as every obligation enumerated above -- they bind simply by declaring 1.9.0, independent of any capability's own status: (a) every operation common_baseline.operations names is executable -- it is not answered with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED, and no capability it needs is declared unavailable; and (b) its capability document carries operation_catalog_url, and the document served at that URL is byte-identical to this contract version's own derived operation catalog. Because common_baseline names operations these capabilities govern, an implementation declaring 1.9.0 declares none of application_catalog, schema_operations, structured_query, atomic_mutation, constraint_declarations, dry_run, idempotency or request_budget as unavailable; every obligation an earlier version made conditional on exactly those capabilities therefore binds unconditionally at 1.9.0, and is not restated here. 1.9.0 introduces no obligation on what a client must send: a request valid under 1.8.0 stays valid. An implementation still declaring 1.8.0 is not held to any 1.9.0-only obligation retroactively. A peer's version-flip -- the commit that changes its own declared contract_version -- must land in the same commit as the real behavior change it claims; declaring a higher version before the corresponding behavior exists, or shipping the behavior while the declaration lags, are both non-conformant.
versioning.obligations_note: obligations is a machine-readable index of what version_binding states in prose: for each version label, the numbered contract decision that introduced it, the obligations that bind unconditionally, and the obligations that bind only where the named capabilities are declared as something other than unavailable. Where an entry names more than one capability, all of them must be so declared for that obligation to bind. This index is derived from version_binding and does not replace it: every limiting clause, exception, same-label addendum and scoping sentence lives in the prose, and where the two could be read as disagreeing, the prose is the contract. The two are held in agreement mechanically -- the set of version labels must match between them, and so must each version's own count of unconditional obligations, where the prose states one.

capability_status.contract_target: Endpoint and schema sections describe peer-target semantics; an implementation publishes its own status for each capability.

defined.structured_query: Structured predicate query over declared entities.
defined.atomic_mutation: Single-entity atomic mutation batches. A capability entry's own operations list names the mutation vocabulary the batch execution surface executes -- not a batch-specific subset distinct from single-operation execution of that same vocabulary. The capability entry schema (CapabilityDocument.capabilities' additionalProperties) is deliberately open, and operations is a peer-published key within that open shape, not a fixed property of the closed envelope -- a client reading only CapabilityDocument's own schema will not find operations declared there; it discovers the key by reading a real capability document.
defined.application_catalog: Catalog discovery of this Application's entities.
defined.audit_query: Audit evidence query under control/audit authority.
defined.best_effort_transactions: Per-item outcome batches with declared partial-result semantics.
defined.idempotency: Request-level idempotency_key deduplication with finite retention bounds.
defined.revision_preconditions: Per-row revision preconditions as defined by structured_operations.revision_preconditions.
defined.row_addressability: Catalog mutation-class declarations and the addressability properties defined by structured_operations.addressability.
defined.cross_entity_mutation: One atomic mutation unit across multiple entities via POST /v1/data/mutations.
defined.constraint_declarations: Declared enum/nullable constraints (SchemaOperationRequest.field_constraints, add_field/alter_field's own enum and nullable) accepted on schema operations and enforced on writes (structured_operations.alter_field, definitions.EntityDescriptor.field_constraints).
defined.dry_run: Request-level dry_run: the same decision the real request would reach, with no externally visible state change (structured_operations.dry_run).
defined.request_budget: A request's own downward-only narrowing of this deployment's declared limits (limits.request_budget).

rules: A capability must not be advertised as enabled unless its operations are executable.
Optional target operations may be unavailable and must fail with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED.
Every discovered finite limit names its enforcement layer; deployment_required is not an application-code proof.

CapabilityDocument.limits and limit_enforcement key names are drawn exclusively from limits.classes; a peer publishing a limit or enforcement entry under a name outside that vocabulary is not conformant. This rule is itself a 1.2.0 obligation (see versioning.version_binding) and does not apply retroactively to an implementation still declaring contract_version 1.1.0.

limit_enforcement values describe the whole deployment reachable at the declared surfaces base URL, never one server process: a peer declares enforced for a limit class only when the bound holds across every process that may serve that base URL at the same time, and declares deployment_required when the bound is held per process and more than one process may serve that base URL.

Optional, in the sense the second rule above gives that word, means outside common_baseline: every operation common_baseline.operations names is required of an implementation declaring the contract version common_baseline.rule binds, and every other target operation stays optional and may be unavailable.

common_baseline.purpose: The operations a client may compose without reading capability_status first. Anything not named here stays optional in the sense capability_status.rules already gives that word.
operations: capability discovery on the data surface (GET /v1/capabilities)
create_entity and add_field under a developer credential, including the enum and nullable members of field_constraints
predicate query with the operators eq, ne, lt, lte, gt, gte and in, together with order_by and the size member of page
predicate-addressed update and delete -- never row-addressed; a delete follows the declare-and-echo protocol destructive_confirmation defines
request-level dry_run and the plan it returns
idempotency_key: the key recorded with its request digest, and a resend of the same key with the same body answered from that record, carrying the original request_id, without executing again
declared enum and nullable constraints enforced on every value written
common_baseline.rule: An implementation declaring this contract version or higher executes every operation named here: it answers none of them with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED, and it declares none of the capabilities common_baseline.capabilities names as unavailable. This is a floor, not a ceiling -- it neither requires nor forbids anything outside the list. A capability declared partial stays conformant as long as its own unsupported list names nothing this list names, and as long as the operations list it publishes to a credential of the role an operation names here carries that operation: schema_operations, for instance, is read under a developer credential, which is the credential this list names for create_entity and add_field. The request_id and details obligations 1.7.0 already binds unconditionally continue to apply to every operation named here. The floor is about what a deployment provides, not about what one entity's own catalog declaration admits: where row_addressability is provided, mutation_classes.rule continues to decide each entity, and an entity declaring a class that does not support update or delete still refuses them with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED -- a refusal the client reads from the catalog before sending, not one it must discover by trying.
common_baseline.outside: Named here to remove doubt, these are NOT in the floor and remain governed by each implementation's own declaration: the contains, matches and is_null operators; upsert; cross-entity mutation; row_addressability (mutation classes and row addresses); revision_preconditions; audit_query on the data surface; best_effort_transactions; create_index, drop_index, drop_entity and jobs; and page.cursor and the continuation a non-null next_page would offer -- a peer may always answer next_page: null.

query.semantics: Entity and fields are validated identifiers; predicates/operators are from the structured allowlist; values are bound, never executable text.

mutate.semantics: A batch is atomic unless explicitly declared best_effort by a capability that defines partial-result semantics. The body carries no entity field; a body entity field is rejected as an unknown field.

cross_entity_mutate.semantics: One atomic unit across entities within the authenticated Application's storage scope. Validation of every operation across every entity completes before any execution begins. Availability is declared via the cross_entity_mutation capability; the entity count is bounded by batch_entities and the operation count by batch_items. batch_entities bounds the number of distinct entity names referenced across operations[]: the same entity may appear in more than one operation, and total operation count remains bounded by batch_items independently of how many distinct entities those operations touch. Each ScopedMutation carries the same per-operation rules as the per-entity Mutation -- including the entity's declared mutation_class gate, upsert's unique_key, expected_revision, and destructive confirmation -- as destructive_confirmation.applies_to's own explicit inclusion of ScopedMutation.operation == "delete" already establishes for the destructive case.

schema.semantics: Schema changes are structured and attributable; destructive changes require explicit destructive semantics and appropriate authority.

audit_query.semantics: Application credentials are denied. Emission is a service consequence and cannot be authored by an application caller.
audit_query.deprecation_note: this entry's path is retained as an alias of control_endpoints.audit_query for one further minor version after 1.4.0, resolving to the identical operation on the control surface's own host, not this section's application surface. audit_query's canonical classification is control_endpoints.audit_query; a client should prefer POST /control/v1/audit/query going forward. This entry is not removed here (removal would be a non-additive contract change) -- it is retained, unmodified in method/request/response shape, specifically so a pre-1.4.0-shaped client is not broken by the reclassification.

operation_catalog.semantics: Served by an implementation declaring 1.9.0 or higher; an implementation declaring a lower version is not held to it.

issue_credential.semantics: Issues an application credential (runtime or developer). The secret appears exactly once, in this response. A role=control issuance request is refused with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED: control-credential issuance exists only in the out-of-band bootstrap/reset ceremony. The role value control remains in the request schema so that a future contract change lifting this restriction is additive. A deployment may freeze credential issuance per application (an out-of-band operation); an issuance request for a frozen application is refused with FORBIDDEN. The freeze refusal is evaluated after the role=control capability refusal (capability refusal precedes application-existence/state/limit resolution, matching C-14 vector 3's normative reading).

rotate_credential.semantics: Replaces the same credential's secret. The replaced secret's invalidation is effective when this response succeeds and propagates within authorization_propagation_bound_ms; no overlap window is defined.

revoke_credential.semantics: Terminal. A revoked credential can never be made valid again; enable does not apply. Revoking the last remaining active control credential is permitted but requires a valid confirmation per the destructive_confirmation section's definition. Every other revocation -- an application credential, or a control credential that is not the last active one -- requires no confirmation.

enable_credential.semantics: Reverses disable only. A revoked credential is not resurrected.

audit_query.semantics: Added in 1.4.0: this is audit_query's canonical location, moved here from endpoints.audit_query because its only real authority (control or audit) and its only real host (the control surface, per control_plane.separability) are both control-plane-shaped, not application-shaped -- endpoints.audit_query's own path (POST /v1/audit/query) remains valid as an alias of this identical operation for one further minor version after 1.4.0 (endpoints.audit_query.deprecation_note). Application credentials are denied. Emission is a service consequence and cannot be authored by an application caller. Where audit_query is provided at all, this path and its alias resolve to the same handler and the same response; where it is unavailable, both still authenticate and authorize the caller before answering CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED (never a bare 404) -- see control_plane.provision and versioning.version_binding's 1.4.0 conditional-obligation list.

endpoint_fields_note.roles: roles lists the roles an endpoint accepts a credential of, restating auth in the vocabulary of security.roles (application meaning both runtime and developer). Being accepted is not a promise of success: an accepted role is still subject to every other gate the endpoint applies, and auth remains the prose the two are held in agreement with.
endpoint_fields_note.requires_capability: requires_capability names the capabilities a deployment must declare as something other than unavailable for the endpoint to be provided at all; where a deployment declares any of them unavailable, the endpoint is not provided and a request to it is refused with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED. It does not list the capabilities that merely extend an endpoint when present -- dry_run, idempotency, request_budget and constraint_declarations -- which are discovered from the capability document and from versioning.obligations.
endpoint_fields_note.atomicity: atomicity places each endpoint under transactions: atomic (one atomic unit per request), none (a read, or a control operation that declares no unit), or atomic_unless_best_effort (atomic unless a capability declaring best_effort semantics is invoked for that request).

control_plane.provision: Providing the control surface is optional. Availability is declared via the control_plane capability; a deployment that declares applications statically and provides no control surface is conformant, and unprovided operations fail with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED.
control_plane.separability: The control surface must be deployable separately from the application surface. The contract does not require co-hosting; where co-hosted, SI-00 conformance evidence must address how the boundary between the surfaces is preserved.
control_plane.authority: Application credentials fail closed on every control endpoint; control credentials are rejected on data/schema endpoints. An audit credential is accepted only on the read-only control_capabilities, list_applications, list_credentials, and audit_query endpoints; every other control endpoint fails it closed with FORBIDDEN.
control_plane.issuance: Only runtime and developer credentials are issuable in-band. Control credentials are created solely by the out-of-band bootstrap or reset ceremony; an in-band role=control issuance request is refused with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED (not a schema violation, so that lifting the restriction later is an additive capability change). Audit credentials, like control credentials, are issued only via the out-of-band ceremony.
control_plane.identifiers: application_id uses the stricter lowercase slug rule (^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,32}$), deliberately narrower than structured_operations.identifier: an application_id becomes platform namespace material (database and role names) in implementations, where case-folding and length decoration make the general identifier rule unsafe.
control_plane.application_deletion: Not defined in v1; disable is the terminal application state. A future deletion capability is a separate contract change bound to destructive semantics and must not sever audit linkage.
bootstrap: Runs under operator/OS authority and is not reachable from any public HTTP surface.
No default or hardcoded credential exists.
While a control credential exists, bootstrap cannot run again without an explicit reset.
The initial control credential is not permanent: it expires or requires rotation; the mechanism is implementation-free.
reset: Revokes every existing control credential; a reset that leaves prior control credentials valid would be a second issuance path that survives revocation.
Destroys neither Application data nor audit evidence.
A credential issued by reset follows the same non-permanence rule as the bootstrap credential.
control_plane.bounds: The control surface publishes its own limits and limit_enforcement via control discovery. Application count, credentials per application, and control operation rate are finite (limits classes: applications, credentials_per_application, control_requests_per_minute).

destructive_confirmation.resolved_in: 1.2.0. Defines the declare-and-echo confirmation semantics for every destructive operation in this contract, common across data, schema, and control-plane surfaces.
applies_to: CredentialRevokeRequest revoking the last remaining active control credential
future destructive operations inherit this same definition

denial.when: A target operation (see applies_to) is presented without a valid confirmation (see valid_confirmation); the request is rejected in full and no operation in it is executed -- there is no partial-application reading of this denial.
denial.details_keys_note: These four keys are a code-specific vocabulary for DESTRUCTIVE_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED, defined here rather than in errors.details_vocabulary; they are additional to, not a replacement for, that section's own common_optional keys (audited/attribution/futility may still appear alongside them on the same denial, as errors.details_vocabulary itself cross-references back to this section).
details_rules: All four keys are present on every denial; omitting one is not conformant.
required_confirmation and consequence are non-empty strings.

reversible_alternative and recovery are each either a non-empty string or null. null declares that no such alternative/recovery genuinely exists for this operation; it is not a stand-in for 'unknown' and is not interchangeable with omitting the key.

A null's truthfulness (an implementation claiming null while a real alternative or recovery path exists) cannot be verified by this mechanism or by conformance testing against it alone; truthful use of null is carried by the implementation's own security-invariant obligations, not by this section.

When a single request presents more than one operation that would each independently require confirmation, the denial names only the first such operation encountered, not every one. An operation-identifying field (e.g. an operation_index) is reserved as a future additive extension and is not required in 1.2.0.

destructive_confirmation.valid_confirmation: A confirmation is valid only when destructive is true (a missing destructive field is equivalent to false, never to true) AND confirmation equals the server's currently-recomputed required_confirmation as an exact Unicode code point sequence, compared after JSON decoding, with no normalization, case-folding, or trimming. Partial match, prefix/suffix match, or a bare presence/non-empty/truthy check does not satisfy this rule; an implementation applying any of those is not conformant.

rules: Derived only from the operation, the target -- including the operation's own scope -- and the consequence class. The request's own destructive/confirmation field values, request_id, timestamps, and any other per-request incidental data are never derivation inputs. Consequently, two requests that are identical except for whether or what confirmation they supply obtain the same phrase -- this is what 'the same request' means everywhere in this section.
Deterministic: recomputing the phrase for the same request always yields the same phrase. The server holds no confirmation state (no stored token, no expiry, no new SI-08 resource).

Scope-included: the target's description in the phrase includes the operation's own scope (e.g., for delete, the selection/where predicate); a request whose scope differs from an otherwise-identical request obtains a different phrase. Exact scope encoding is implementation-defined (see spelling below), but two different scopes must never collide onto the same phrase.

State-fingerprinted for re-creatable targets: a target identifiable by a name that can be destroyed and later recreated (e.g. an entity or index) includes a state fingerprint in its phrase, so that either the target's re-creation under the same name, or any other schema change, invalidates any previously valid phrase for that name -- recreating the identical structure under the same name after a drop does not resurrect an old phrase's validity.

Only identifier-validated target names: a phrase never reflects an unvalidated client-supplied string back to the client; every target name appearing in a phrase has already passed this implementation's own identifier validation.

Bounded: a phrase always fits within confirmation's maxLength. A target whose faithful, literal description would exceed that bound is instead named via a bounded, deterministic digest -- this contract does not bound identifier length, so this escape is required to keep every otherwise-legal request expressible.
phrase_construction.spelling: Exact phrase spelling is implementation-defined and is not fixed or standardized by this contract; only the construction rules above are normative. Spelling is therefore not a cross-implementation compatibility surface (see client_obligation).

destructive_confirmation.evaluation_order: Confirmation validity is evaluated after shape validation, authentication/authorization, and target-existence checks, and before precondition evaluation and execution.
destructive_confirmation.client_obligation: A client obtains required_confirmation from the denial's own declaration and echoes it back verbatim on the next attempt. Guessing, memorizing, or hardcoding a phrase is not a supported integration pattern; a future implementation changing its phrase spelling (while still following phrase_construction's rules) is not a breaking change.
destructive_confirmation.non_destructive_requests: destructive and confirmation remain ordinary, schema-validated optional fields and are never inspected on a request that carries no destructive-confirmation semantics -- including a revoke_credential request that does not meet the last-active-control-credential condition.
destructive_confirmation.scope_limit: This mechanism only removes ambiguity about which destructive operation, on which target, a caller is confirming -- it proves the caller received and echoed the server's own current declaration for this exact request. It does not, and is not intended to, defend against an unintended or malicious request issued with valid credentials that supplies a correctly-guessed, memorized, or hardcoded phrase: deterministic phrases can be embedded in client scripts, and this mechanism's real-world effectiveness depends on a caller that reads the server's declaration rather than one that never varies its input. That residual risk, where addressed at all, is addressed by controls outside this mechanism (e.g. reversibility, durable audit, credential-lifecycle discipline) -- not by this section.

applies_to_structured.condition: revoking the last remaining active control credential

applies_to_structured.note: future destructive operations inherit this same definition

query_operators.contains: Literal substring containment, case-sensitive: every character of the value is matched verbatim, and no character of the value is interpreted as a wildcard or pattern token.
query_operators.matches: Wildcard pattern match, case-sensitive: % matches any sequence including the empty one, _ matches exactly one character, and a backslash escapes the next character. A pattern ending in an unescaped backslash has no next character to escape and is refused with VALIDATION_FAILED. An implementation not providing matches refuses it with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED; it is never silently interpreted as a different operator.
query_operators.case_folding: Neither operator folds case; a case-insensitive comparison would be a separate additive operator.

structured_operations.identifier: ASCII letters, digits, and underscore; first character must be a letter or underscore; implementation may apply a stricter known-catalog policy.
structured_operations.reserved_entity_names_note: audit_events is reserved across implementations as an entity/collection name, for platform-managed audit storage an implementation may keep alongside application-declared entities in the same underlying storage. This documents an existing implementation practice (both peers already refuse this exact name defensively) rather than introducing new behavior; a client entity/schema operation naming audit_events is refused (a validation-class error; the exact contract code is implementation-defined) rather than silently colliding with platform storage. This list is additive: a future implementation-shared reserved name may be appended without removing this one.
structured_operations.values: JSON values are passed through a parameter-binding boundary; values are never interpolated into native command text.
structured_operations.sql: No public operation accepts SQL, database-native command text, scripts, or connection credentials.
structured_operations.scope: The target Application is the authenticated credential's server-derived scope. A client application_id, database, schema, or role field is not authority.

mutation_classes.rule: Where row_addressability is enabled, every entity declares one mutation class in the catalog, and a declared class rejects every mutation it does not support with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED. delete under append_delete is set semantics (all rows matching the predicate); an entity that needs guaranteed single-row deletion declares the mutable class.
mutation_classes.declaration_required: There is no default for an undeclared entity: an implementation must not advertise row_addressability as enabled until every entity carries a declaration.

properties: Declared: the catalog entry names the field set that constitutes the row address.
Visible: address fields are ordinary selectable fields and appear in query results.
Targetable: a where+eq over the full address set matches at most one row; a write that would duplicate an address set fails with CONFLICT.
Immutable: address values do not change during a row's lifetime; an update that modifies an address field fails with VALIDATION_FAILED.

No spontaneous reassignment: a retired address is reassigned only as the result of explicit client mutations (delete then insert); maintenance operations (compaction, vacuum, rebuild, restart) never renumber or reassign addresses. Conformance evidence combines automated tests over inducible disturbances with review evidence over maintenance paths.
addressability.reuse_declaration: Every mutable entity's catalog entry declares whether a retired address can be reused by a later insert (address_reuse: never or possible); a client reads the declaration to decide whether revision preconditions are required for its access pattern.
addressability.assigned_identifiers: Server-assigned address values returned by MutationResult are Application-scoped; their values and increments must not permit inferring another Application's existence or activity. Each assigned_addresses element carries the created row's address-field values under address, one element per insert (and upsert resolving to insert) in operation order; on the cross-entity endpoint the element also names its entity.

structured_operations.upsert: upsert's existence test is the entity's declared domain uniqueness: a key created by create_index with unique true, surfaced in the catalog as the EntityDescriptor's unique_keys. upsert on an entity without a declared uniqueness key fails with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED; and, where row_addressability is provided (other than unavailable) -- the same precondition mutation_classes.rule carries for the declaration itself -- upsert or update on an entity not declaring the mutable class fails with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED as well. An implementation that does not provide row_addressability does not thereby declare a mutation class for any entity, and this sentence does not refuse the mutations its own atomic_mutation capability declares. Where an entity declares more than one uniqueness key, the operation names the deciding key in its unique_key field using the catalog key name; with exactly one declared key, unique_key may be omitted and defaults to that key. An upsert omitting unique_key on an entity with multiple declared keys fails with VALIDATION_FAILED (the existence test would be ambiguous), a unique_key naming no declared key fails with NOT_FOUND, and unique_key on any operation other than upsert fails with VALIDATION_FAILED. On an entity with no declared uniqueness key, upsert fails with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED regardless of any unique_key field (the capability check precedes key-name resolution).

clauses: A revision is an implementation-issued opaque string; clients do not interpret its content.
Its scope is one row; it is distinct from any entity schema revision.
It changes every time a mutation of that row commits.
It does not change on mutations of other rows.
The expected_revision comparison is atomic with the mutation.

A mismatch fails with PRECONDITION_FAILED. A missing target row fails with NOT_FOUND for update and delete, and for upsert when no uniqueness match exists (a precondition asserts a known existing row; it is never silently ignored by resolving to insert). expected_revision on insert fails with VALIDATION_FAILED. Without expected_revision, an update or delete matching zero rows remains a success with affected 0; NOT_FOUND applies only when a precondition asserted existence.
revision_preconditions.query_results: An implementation advertising revision_preconditions as enabled returns row revisions alongside query results (QueryResult.revisions, index-aligned with items) for entities of the append_delete and mutable classes — the classes that support row mutation and can therefore use a precondition. read_only and append_only entities carry no revisions: a recomputed read-only projection has no stable row for a revision to name, and requiring one there would gate the very class those declarations exist to admit. Implementations not advertising the capability are not required to maintain revisions.

dry_run.decision: dry_run asks the service to reach the same decision it would reach for the identical request without it, and then to leave nothing behind. A dry-run request is subject to the same gates a real one is -- authentication, role, request rate and concurrency, request size, operation depth, request shape, capability availability, and validation -- and any refusal it receives is the refusal the real request would receive, with the same code and the same details: authorization refusals, destructive-confirmation refusals, precondition refusals and limit refusals are all part of what a dry run decides, not steps it skips. Where it is not refused, it answers with the same response schema the real request answers with, carrying committed: false, the affected count the real request would have produced, and a plan. A dry-run mutation does not carry assigned_addresses: the addresses a real execution would assign are not settled, and reporting them would be a false statement rather than a preview. A dry-run schema operation carries descriptor, the EntityDescriptor the entity would have afterwards. Its revision is the Application's schema revision as it stands now -- the revision the plan was taken against -- and not the revision the operation would establish, which for the same reason assigned_addresses is withheld is not settled until it commits.
dry_run.external_effects: A dry run leaves no externally visible state change: no row, no catalog entry, no schema revision, no idempotency record, and no audit event is created, changed or removed by it. Two consumptions are deliberately outside that statement. First, a dry run is a request, and consumes this deployment's own request-rate and concurrency bounds exactly as a real request does -- a bound a client could avoid by asking for a dry run would not be a bound. Second, where an implementation assigns addresses from a non-transactional sequence, a dry run may consume a value from that sequence; it never returns the value it consumed, and the consumed value is not reused, which is what EntityDescriptor.address_reuse: never already declares. An idempotency_key presented on a dry-run request is neither recorded nor looked up: the dry run is not deduplicated against earlier requests, and does not make a later resend of the same key a duplicate. This is stated rather than left to the reader as "ignored", because a client that resends after a dry run must be able to know that its first real send is genuinely the first.
dry_run.plan: plan is an opaque but deterministic token: it is computed from the request itself together with the Application's own schema revision -- the same value SchemaOperationResult.revision reports -- as it stood when the request was decided, and holds no server-side state -- there is nothing on the service that expires, is evicted, or must be cleaned up, and two dry runs of the identical request against unchanged schema return the identical token. The token is computed over this request as this contract defines it -- the request object this endpoint's own request schema names, not the bytes a particular transport delivered it in -- taking every field of that object except plan itself, which cannot contain its own digest, and dry_run, whose value necessarily differs between the dry run and the real request it plans. Every other field, including budget, transaction, confirmation and idempotency_key, is part of what the token commits to: a real request differing from the dry run in any of them is a different request, and the token no longer agrees. The digest is taken over that object serialized with its keys in lexicographic order, without insignificant whitespace, and without escaping non-ASCII characters, as UTF-8; the token an implementation returns is its own representation of that digest together with the revision. A client may present the token it received back on the real request. Where it does, the service recomputes the token by the same rule and executes only if the two agree; where they disagree -- because the request differs, or because any schema operation on that Application advanced its revision in between -- the request is refused with PRECONDITION_FAILED and details.violated_declaration: plan, and nothing is executed. Because that revision is the Application's own, a schema operation on any entity of the same Application invalidates a plan taken against any other: the token names the Application's schema state, not one entity's. A plan is a precondition, and is evaluated where destructive_confirmation.evaluation_order places precondition evaluation -- after confirmation validity and before execution -- so a request that is both unconfirmed and carrying a stale plan is refused for the missing confirmation first. A plan is never required: a real request that omits it executes on the service's own current state, exactly as it did before this version.

idempotency.record: An idempotency_key is recorded together with a deterministic digest of the request it was sent with, and the record is written in the same transaction as the effects it records: a key is present exactly when the request it names committed. A request that fails leaves no record, so resending it is a new attempt, not a duplicate. Within idempotency_retention_ms of the recorded request, resending the same key with the same request digest returns that original request's own recorded result -- the whole MutationResult or SchemaOperationResult, including its request_id -- without executing anything a second time. Resending the same key with a different request digest is refused with CONFLICT and details.violated_declaration: idempotency_key; the denial does not disclose the earlier request. A key whose retention has elapsed is treated as absent: the resend is a new request, and an implementation may delete elapsed records lazily. A key is scoped to one Application: the same key presented under a different credential of the same Application is the same key, because the atomic unit this contract defines is scoped to one Application's storage. Where recording a new key would exceed idempotency_entries after elapsed records are reclaimed, the request is refused with LIMIT_EXCEEDED and details.limit_class: idempotency_entries, before it executes rather than after. A replayed SchemaOperationResult carries the revision the original execution produced, which is the revision that execution established, not necessarily the entity's revision now. The digest is taken over the request object this endpoint's own request schema names, excluding idempotency_key itself, plan and dry_run, and is otherwise computed exactly as structured_operations.dry_run.plan describes: every other field, including budget, transaction and confirmation, is part of what a resend must match. A resend that matches a retained record is answered from that record before target existence, destructive confirmation and any precondition are evaluated -- after this request's own authentication, authorization and bounds, which it consumes like any other request. Without that placement a resent destructive operation could not be answered from its record at all: its target no longer exists, and destructive_confirmation.phrase_construction recomputes a phrase against state the first execution already changed. This holds for concurrent sends as well: two requests carrying the same key that arrive together are serialized by the implementation so that at most one of them executes; the other is answered after the first commits as a resend -- from the record where the digests agree, with CONFLICT where they differ -- or, where the first failed and left no record, executes as a new request. The idempotency_entries bound is evaluated under that same serialization, so two concurrent requests recording different keys cannot both pass a check that only one of them would pass in sequence.
idempotency.correlation: Idempotency and audit evidence are correlated through request_id, not through the key: a resend answers with the original execution's own request_id, which is the identifier that execution's audit events carry, so a client holding only its own responses can tell which single execution its repeated sends resolved to. The key itself is not written to audit events.
idempotency.key_secrecy: A client MUST NOT place a credential, token, password, private key, or any other secret in an idempotency_key. The key is not a member of audit.forbidden_fields, and this version writes it neither to audit events nor to any response -- but neither of those facts makes a secret safe to use as a key. A key is a client-chosen name for one request, is compared for equality against other clients' keys within the same Application, and may be retained for as long as idempotency_retention_ms declares; a value that must not be guessable, resent, or retained does not belong in it.

structured_operations.alter_field: alter_field redeclares the constraints of one existing field: it sets, replaces or clears that field's enum, and switches its nullable. It does not redeclare that field's type -- an alter_field carrying field_type fails VALIDATION_FAILED -- because converting values already stored under one type into another is not defined by this version. Before it changes anything, an alter_field verifies every existing row of the entity against the constraints it would establish, within the same transaction as the change itself; where even one row would violate them, the whole operation is refused with CONFLICT and nothing is changed. The denial names the field and which declaration it would violate, and never the offending values, nor how many rows there are. A committed alter_field advances the entity's schema revision. A constraint the request omits is left as it is; enum: null clears the field's enum, and on add_field enum: null means the same as omitting it. An add_field declaring nullable: false on an entity that already holds rows is refused with CONFLICT on the same rule, because every existing row would hold null in the new field. An alter_field carrying neither enum nor nullable declares nothing and is refused with VALIDATION_FAILED; it does not advance the schema revision.

transactions.atomic: All operations in the declared atomic unit commit together or leave no externally visible partial state.
transactions.best_effort: Only a capability that declares best_effort may return per-item outcomes; the contract must identify partial effects.
transactions.cross_entity: The cross_entity_mutation capability executes one atomic unit across entities within a single Application's storage scope. Cross-Application atomicity is not defined. Validation of every operation across every entity completes before any execution begins.
transactions.interactive: No interactive transaction surface (begin/commit held open across client round trips) is defined in v1; the atomic unit is a single request. Holding locks and connections across client round trips is an SI-08 hazard. Reconsideration: a design that structurally proves finite bounds on cross-round-trip resource holding may be reviewed as a separate contract change.
transactions.retry: Clients use idempotency_key, revision preconditions, or explicit conflict handling; retries do not silently widen scope.

errors.disclosure: No credential material, SQL, row values, stack traces, database names, role names, connection details, or sensitive existence distinctions are returned. Safe field-level diagnostics remain allowed.
errors.http_status_note: DESTRUCTIVE_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED's HTTP status (409) is specified in destructive_confirmation.denial.http_status. Where this contract does not specify an HTTP status for another code, that status is undefined by this contract -- not left to arbitrary per-implementation choice -- and cross-peer HTTP status agreement for those codes is tracked as conformance evidence outside this document, not fixed here.

details_vocabulary.cross_reference: DESTRUCTIVE_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED's own details keys (required_confirmation, consequence, reversible_alternative, recovery) are defined in the destructive_confirmation section's denial.details_keys, not here; they are a separate, code-specific vocabulary from LIMIT_EXCEEDED.limit_class and the common_optional keys below, which may still appear alongside them on the same denial.

LIMIT_EXCEEDED.limit_class: string, required. Must be a member of limits.classes -- the specific finite-resource class this request exceeded.

common_optional.audited: boolean, optional, present only when true: this denial was durably recorded as a canonical audit event. Never asserted as false; its absence carries no meaning about whether audit recording happened for this denial.
common_optional.attribution: string, optional: a safe, non-secret description of who/what a durably-recorded denial is attributed to (e.g. the acting credential's role).
common_optional.futility: string, optional: a safe, non-secret statement of why retrying this exact request would not succeed.

details_vocabulary.open: details is not a closed vocabulary: any error code's denial may carry declared keys beyond those named here, and this codification is not an exhaustive enumeration -- it names the keys this version defines, leaving room for future additive declarations. SI-10's non-disclosure requirement constrains what any details value may contain regardless of key name; it is a restriction on content, not a license to treat undocumented key freedom as safe by default.

VALIDATION_FAILED.violated_declaration: string, required. Which declaration this request violated, drawn from errors.details_vocabulary.violated_declaration_vocabulary.
VALIDATION_FAILED.field: string, required whenever the violation is attributable to one position in the request: that position, named as a '/'-separated path from the request body root, with no leading separator (for example operations/0/values/label, budget/result_items, or entity). It names a position in the request, never a storage location.
VALIDATION_FAILED.declared_type: string, required where violated_declaration is field_type or nullable, and where it is request_schema and the violation is about a value's type -- the type the declaration names, a member of the field-type vocabulary for a field-level violation or the JSON type this contract's own request schema names for a request-shape one. Where violated_declaration is enum, it names the field's own declared type; where the violation is an unrecognized field, no type is declared for it and this key is absent.
VALIDATION_FAILED.observed_type: string, required alongside declared_type wherever declared_type is required, except under enum, where the value's own type is not what was violated and this key is omitted so that an enum violation is not read as a type mismatch: the JSON type of the value actually received (string, integer, number, boolean, object, array or null), or absent where the request omitted a value the declaration requires.

IDENTIFIER_INVALID.field: string, required. The position in the request carrying the identifier, named as for VALIDATION_FAILED.field.

CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED.field: string, required whenever the unsupported operation or field occupies a determinate position in the request, named as for VALIDATION_FAILED.field; omitted where the request as a whole is what is unsupported.

details_vocabulary.violated_declaration_vocabulary: A closed vocabulary of eleven values naming which declaration a denial reports as violated: request_schema (the request does not match this contract's own request schema for that endpoint), identifier_syntax (an identifier does not match the identifier syntax this contract declares), field_type (a value does not match the field's declared type), enum (a non-null value is not a member of the field's declared enum), nullable (a null was written to, or a required value omitted from, a field declared nullable: false), capability (this deployment does not provide the operation or field the request names), budget (the request's own budget declaration is itself invalid -- a class that does not apply to this endpoint, a value above the deployed bound, or a non-integer), unsupported_field (a field this version gives no meaning to, carried where the request schema can still receive it), plan (a plan token does not match the request and schema state it is presented against), idempotency_key (the same key was resent with a different request digest), and constraint_declaration (a field_constraints, enum or nullable declaration is itself invalid: an enum on a field whose type admits none, an empty or duplicated enum, a member outside the field's declared type, or a declaration naming a field the request does not create). The required-key rules above bind VALIDATION_FAILED, IDENTIFIER_INVALID and CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED only; any other code's denial may carry violated_declaration drawn from this same vocabulary without being required to -- PRECONDITION_FAILED carries plan, and CONFLICT carries idempotency_key, or enum/nullable where an alter_field is refused because existing rows would violate the constraints it declares. Every value a details key carries under this vocabulary is a statement of declared fact: never a row value, never a suggested value, never a corrective action, never SQL, and never an internal name (SI-10 constrains the content of every details value regardless of key name, as errors.details_vocabulary.open already states).
details_vocabulary.layer_rule: The four keys above are decided by the layer that reads the declaration -- the request-shape check and the value-validation choke point. An implementation may keep additional defence-in-depth validation behind those layers; such a layer is not required to produce these keys, and a denial reaching a client without them is evidence that the declaration-reading layer did not run first.

limits.profile: Limits are deployment-profile values and are returned by capability discovery. Enforcement scope is the deployment behind the declared base URL (capability_status.rules); a bound kept in per-process memory is enforced for the deployment only while exactly one process serves that base URL.
limits.audit_requests_per_minute_note: A pre-authentication fixed window governing the audit_query endpoint specifically (both its canonical and alias paths, control_endpoints.audit_query/endpoints.audit_query.deprecation_note), separate from control_requests_per_minute: an implementation publishing this class enforces it as audit_query's own window and does not also charge audit_query requests against control_requests_per_minute, so that a high-frequency audit_query poller cannot exhaust the same window a break-glass control-plane operation (e.g. revoke_credential) depends on.
limits.enum_members: enum_members bounds how many members one field's declared enum may carry. It counts members, not bytes: the length of any single member is bounded by request_bytes on the schema operation that declares it, as every other request-carried string is. A create_entity, add_field or alter_field declaring an enum with more members than this deployment's own declared value is refused with LIMIT_EXCEEDED and details.limit_class: enum_members, before anything is created or altered. The bound is per field: an entity may declare an enum on every one of its fields, each within this bound, subject to schema_objects as before.
limits.request_budget: budget lets one request ask for a smaller bound than the deployment's own, and only a smaller one. Where a request carries budget.<class>, the bound in force for that request is the smaller of the deployment's declared value for that class and the requested value; a request whose budget.<class> exceeds the deployment's own declared value is refused with VALIDATION_FAILED and details.violated_declaration: budget, rather than being silently reduced -- a client that asked for more than the deployment allows has misread the deployment's own declaration, and telling it so is more useful than granting it less than it asked for. Exceeding a bound that is in force because a budget narrowed it is refused exactly as exceeding the deployed bound is: LIMIT_EXCEEDED with details.limit_class naming that class, without distinguishing which of the two values was the smaller. Three classes are budgetable in this version: result_items, execution_ms and batch_items. Each applies only where it has meaning: result_items and execution_ms on a query; execution_ms and batch_items on a single-entity or cross-entity mutation; execution_ms alone on a schema operation. result_items is not budgetable on a mutation: it bounds the rows a query returns, and this version does not give one request a way to narrow how many rows its own mutation may affect. A budget naming a class that does not apply to the endpoint it was sent to, or carrying a value that is not an integer of at least 1, is refused with VALIDATION_FAILED, details.violated_declaration: budget and details.field naming that class within budget; it is not ignored. Every one of those refusals belongs to validating the request itself: a budget is checked where this contract's own request shape is checked, before target existence, destructive confirmation and precondition evaluation, so a request that is both unconfirmed and carrying an invalid budget is refused for the budget first. budget never raises a bound, never introduces a class outside limits.classes, and never changes what this deployment declares at capability discovery -- the declared values remain the deployment's own, and a budget is one request's own narrowing of them.

lifecycle.credential: Control authority may issue, rotate, revoke, disable, or enable credentials. Revocation is terminal: a revoked credential can never be made valid again, and enable reverses disable only. Disable/enable are reversible operational states. Rotation replaces the same credential's secret; the replaced secret's invalidation is effective when the rotate response succeeds. A revoked credential is rejected on subsequent authorization after the documented propagation bound.
lifecycle.application: A disabled Application rejects all application-facing operations; authorization state unavailable for a protected operation fails closed.
lifecycle.user_session: Where Application User/Identity is enabled, user/session status and policy are server-bound and revocation is fail-closed within the published bound.
lifecycle.propagation_bound: Each deployment publishes a finite authorization-state propagation bound in its profile; indefinite stale authorization is non-conformant.

audit.emission: The service emits canonical attributable events for authentication/authorization denials, lifecycle changes, destructive and privilege-sensitive operations, and security-control failures.
audit.sink_failure_policy: Failure to durably record an authentication/authorization denial, a credential or Application lifecycle change, a destructive or privilege-sensitive operation, or a security-control failure fails the operation closed. Failure to record an ordinary data-operation event may be absorbed by a bounded buffer that raises an explicit operational alert; it must not silently discard events without that alert.
audit.fields_note: audit.fields is an additive vocabulary, not a mandatory column set. target_id is an OPTIONAL per-event field, present when the event has a single target credential or application, absent otherwise.
audit.immutability: Application authority cannot author, override, update, or delete security evidence. The sink is append-only and externally governed where required by the deployment.
audit.query_authority: Audit evidence query is separate from emission and requires control/audit authority.
audit.query_ordering: AuditResult.events[] returned by audit_query is totally ordered by (recorded_at, plane, event_id). plane is included in the ordering key because an implementation may hold more than one durable event source (e.g. a control-plane source and an application-plane source) whose own event_id vocabularies are not mutually unique, so recorded_at and plane together, not event_id alone, are what make the combined order total.
audit.query_cursor: AuditQueryRequest.after is an opaque cursor, not an event_id or a numeric offset -- a client never constructs one itself, only echoes back the cursor field of the last event it received (query_event_fields_note). A cursor that fails to decode, or that no longer resolves under the request's own filters, is refused with VALIDATION_FAILED. A cursor obtained under one set of filters is valid only when reused with that same set of filters; reusing it under different filters is not defined by this version.
audit.query_event_fields_note: each event AuditResult.events[] returns from audit_query MAY carry fields beyond audit.fields -- plane (control or application: the durable source the event was read from, never a value the original event-writer could itself set), recorded_at (when the event became durable, distinct from the emission-time occurred_at already in audit.fields), cursor (this event's own opaque position, suitable for a later after), and count (present only on an event representing more than one coalesced occurrence, absent -- never zero or one -- otherwise). AuditResult.events[] remains an open per-event shape, so none of these are a schema-breaking addition.
audit.query_event_class_vocabulary: event_class is a vocabulary each implementation declares for itself, at capabilities().audit_query.event_classes -- this contract does not enumerate a fixed event_class enum, and does not require an implementation's declared vocabulary to include any particular member (declare-the-hazard, matching audit.fields' own additive-vocabulary posture rather than capability_status.defined's closed status_enum).
audit.query_operation_vocabulary: operations and target_kinds are vocabularies each implementation declares for itself at capabilities().audit_query.operations / .target_kinds -- the sets of values the operation and target_kind fields of events returned by audit_query can take. As with event_classes, this contract enumerates no fixed enum and requires no particular member (declare-the-hazard). An implementation declaring 1.5.0 or higher whose audit_query is other than unavailable MUST declare both, and every event it returns MUST carry values drawn from the declared sets; the same superset relation holds for event_classes, stated here explicitly. audit_query.operations is the vocabulary of the audit row's operation field and is unrelated to capability_status.defined.atomic_mutation.operations, which enumerates the executable mutation verbs.
