field_types.description: The field-type vocabulary gains a seventh member, json, meaning any JSON value. A field created without a declared type has type json -- this names an existing default rather than introducing a new one, and there is no "unknown" member of the vocabulary: every field carries a real type. EntityDescriptor.field_types maps every name in fields to that field's type, drawn from that same vocabulary. What a client declared -- through SchemaOperationRequest.field_types on create_entity, or field_type on add_field -- is what the catalog reports back, and a field for which no type was declared reports json. Where a schema operation later redeclares a field's type, the catalog reports the type most recently declared. The catalog reports only facts this contract's own schema operations can establish: nullability and enum membership through field_constraints, and neither default values nor a notion of required distinct from nullable: false, because no schema operation defined here establishes either; a later version that gives schema operations such a notion gives it to the catalog in that same version. object and array are narrower than json: a field declared json accepts any JSON value, including but not limited to objects and arrays, while a field declared object or array accepts only that shape -- and the catalog reports the narrower word it was declared with, never rounding it up to json. SchemaOperationRequest.field_types and EntityDescriptor.field_types share one object shape but not one coverage rule: the request's object may be partial -- any name in fields that it omits is created with type json -- while the catalog's object is always total over that entity's own fields. SchemaOperationRequest.field_types is never required: a create_entity naming only fields remains a valid request, creating json fields. A field_types naming a field the request's own fields does not name, a field_types value outside this vocabulary, or a field_types sent without fields, each fails VALIDATION_FAILED; none of the three is silently ignored. add_field continues to carry a single field_type for the single field it adds.

field_constraints.description: field_constraints declares, per field, the two constraints this version defines: nullable (whether that field accepts a null value) and enum (the closed set of non-null values that field accepts). On create_entity it is an object keyed by field name and may be partial -- any name in fields it omits is created with no enum and nullable: true. On add_field and alter_field the same two constraints are carried as the request's own top-level enum and nullable, for the single field the operation names. nullable defaults to true, which is what a field created before this version, or created without the key, already is: this names an existing default rather than introducing a new one. A field declared nullable: false requires a non-null value on insert -- an operation that omits it is refused -- and cannot be set to null by update or upsert. An upsert that resolves to an insert is refused on the same rule; an upsert that resolves to an update is not, because it writes no value to that field. enum constrains non-null values only; whether null is accepted is decided by nullable alone, and a field may declare both. An enum is a non-empty list of distinct values, each of the field's own declared type, and is declarable only on a field whose type is string, integer, number or boolean: an enum on an object, array or json field, an empty or duplicated enum, an enum member outside the field's declared type, a field_constraints naming a field the request's own fields does not name, or a field_constraints sent without fields, each fails VALIDATION_FAILED; none of them is silently ignored. Constraints bind writes only: a query predicate is never refused for carrying a value outside a field's enum -- such a value simply matches no row.

CapabilityDocument.description: The envelope itself is closed (additionalProperties: false at this level), but capabilities/limits/limit_enforcement below and each capability entry's own value schema deliberately keep additionalProperties open: an open key space naming deployment-declared capabilities and limit classes is an intentional, distinct mechanism, not an oversight comparable to the closed response envelopes elsewhere in this contract.

surfaces.description: surfaces names the absolute base URLs at which this deployment's own surfaces are reached, as declared by the deployer -- never derived, and never to be inferred by a client from the URL it happened to use. surfaces.data.base_url ends at versioning.base_path; surfaces.control.base_url ends at versioning.control_base_path. The data surface's capability document and the control surface's own capability document return the same surfaces object, so a client holding either base URL can reach the other surface, and either document, fetched again at its own declared URL, answers with the same contract_version and the same surfaces -- the rest of each document remains scoped to the credential presented. A deployment declaring control_plane as unavailable omits surfaces.control. Neither URL ends in a trailing slash, so that appending a path to it yields exactly one separator. Whether the two surfaces share a host is read from the origins (scheme, host and port -- not the path) of these two URLs -- the co-hosting versioning.control_discovery permits -- and is never assumed; where surfaces.control is absent, the surfaces are not co-hosted. Where the two surfaces run as separate processes, both are configured from the same declaration: neither can verify the other's document, so a deployment whose two documents disagree is non-conformant, and a client is given no rule for preferring one over the other.

operation_catalog_url.description: Required of an implementation declaring 1.9.0 or higher: the absolute URL at which a client reaches this deployment's own operation_catalog operation. The document served there is byte-identical to the derived operation catalog of the contract version this capability document declares. The URL is not required to sit under this deployment's surfaces.data.base_url: a deployment serving the document from elsewhere -- a content delivery network, for instance -- names that URL here. An implementation declaring a lower version may publish it or not, as before.

request_id.description: request_id is the service's own identifier for the request this result answers -- the same identifier its audit evidence for that request carries, and the same shape errors.shape.request_id already names on a denial. It is generated by the service; this contract defines no way for a client to supply or influence it. It is declared as an optional property so that a response written under an earlier version remains valid against this schema; an implementation declaring 1.7.0 carries it on every successful QueryResult, MutationResult and SchemaOperationResult it returns (versioning.version_binding). Where a request is answered from an idempotency record rather than executed, the request_id returned is the original execution's own, not a new one (structured_operations.idempotency.correlation).

address.description: Deliberately left open: the address field-name vocabulary is entity-defined (EntityDescriptor.address_fields), not fixed by this contract.

descriptor.description: The entity's descriptor -- as it would read afterwards (dry_run), or as committed.

items.description: audit.fields is itself an open-ended, additive vocabulary, and a per-event shape is not one of the 11 response schemas or nested row schemas this contract closes.

secret.description: CredentialIssued.secret -- and the secret a rotate response returns, wherever this contract defines one -- is the complete bearer token for the surface that credential is for: a client presents that exact string, verbatim, as Authorization: Bearer <secret>; an application credential on the application surface, a control or audit credential on the control surface (security.schemes.control_credential continues to state that application credentials are not accepted there). A client MUST NOT compose it from, split it into, or derive it from any other field of the response -- credential_id is returned as its own field, for naming the credential in later control operations, and is never something a client extracts from the secret. Its internal structure is opaque; an implementation may change that structure without a contract change, and no client may depend on it. The service still stores only a verifier/digest and never returns the secret again.

must_rotate.description: Present for a credential whose issuance ritual has not yet completed (rotate pending); omitted for application credentials, where the concept does not exist.

field_constraints.description: field_constraints reports, for every one of this entity's own fields, the constraints currently in force on it: nullable, always present, and enum, present only on a field that declares one. Like field_types, and unlike the request-side object of the same name, this object is always total over that entity's own fields. What a client declared -- through SchemaOperationRequest.field_constraints on create_entity, or enum/nullable on add_field or alter_field -- is what the catalog reports back, and a field for which nothing was declared reports nullable: true and no enum. This is the same-version catalog reporting the 1.6.0 field_types description reserves for whichever later version gives schema operations a notion of nullability: this is that version, and the notion it gives is exactly these two constraints -- not default values, and no notion of a required field beyond what nullable: false itself requires on insert.
